newsitem.title: UK: INTERVIEW - JKX seeks to show it can deliver.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - JKX seeks to show it can deliver.

text.p: JKX Oil & Gas, the independent exploration group operating exclusively in the former Soviet Union, said on Thursday it hopes first-half results have proved to investors that it can deliver on its promises.
"I'm tring to demonstrate to investors that we can deliver, we can produce and we can get the money out," chief executive David Robson said in a telephone interview with Reuters.

The group, which floated on the stock exchange last year and operates principally in Georgia and the Ukraine, said pre-tax losses in the first six months of the year widened to 1.2 million stg from 0.5 million a year earlier.
JKX was producing an average of 5,700 barrels of oil equivalent (boe) per day at its fields in both of the newly independent countries in the first half of 1996.
There was no production in the comparable period a year before.
Robson said output in September at the Poltava site in the Ukraine was up to 10,400 boe per day and in Georgia averaged 2,350 barrels of oil per day.
Finance director Tony Whyatt told Reuters that capital expenditure in the first six months of the year totalled $14.7 million, mostly spent at Poltava.

He said full-year spending would total around $25 million, and added "we are at the stage now where Poltava could be self-funding." Cash reserves at the end of June stood at 12 million stg, and Whyatt said JKX had injected some debt onto its balance sheet, with gearing standing at around 17 percent.
Robson said JKX, through its 49 percent-owned subsidiary Poltava Petroleum Co (PPC), would drill more appraisal wells over the winter, when it would not disturb Ukrainian farmers.
The first Ukrainian field to be exploited, Novo-Nikolaevskoye, had reserves of around 1.1 trillion cubic feet of gas and 52 million barrels of oil, Robson said.

Robson said output in the Ukraine is sold domestically, with the recently-reformed Ukrainian distribution system greatly helping JKX. The Ukraine, with a size and population similar to that of France, is the world's third-biggest gas consumer, partly because of its heavy industrial base.
Robson said there is "huge future potential" in the Ukraine.
"Young people coming through are very commercially aware.

"The people at the top are reformers, who are trying to lift the Ukraine onto the world stage rather than the Russian stage. The Ukraine wants to become a major free-market force in central Europe," he added.

Robson said Georgia has now stabilised after a turbulent period, with the currency pegged to the mark and the IMF backing economic reforms. JKX oil from Georgia is already being exported to refineries in the eastern Mediterranean, including Greece.

Robson added that JKX's ambitions in Russia are being held back by the lack of product-sharing agreements, whereby contractors pay all the costs of development in return for a proportion of the output.
